speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Good afternoon.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: My colleagues and I remain squarely focused on achieving our dual-mandate goals of maximum employment and stable prices for the benefit of the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The U.S. economy has been expanding at a solid pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: While job gains have remained low, the unemployment rate has been little changed in recent months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation has moved up and is elevated, in part reflecting the recent increase in global energy prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Today, the FOMC decided to leave our policy rate unchanged.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We see the current stance of monetary policy as appropriate to promote progress toward our maximum-employment and 2 percent inflation goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Developments in the Middle East are contributing to a high level of uncertainty about the economic outlook, and we will remain attentive to risks to both sides of our dual mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’ll have more to say about monetary policy after briefly reviewing economic developments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Recent indicators suggest that economic activity has been expanding at a solid pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Consumer spending has been resilient, and business fixed investment has continued to expand at a brisk pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In contrast, activity in the housing sector has remained weak.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In the labor market, the unemployment rate was 4.3 percent in March and has changed little in recent months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Job gains have remained low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: A good part of the slowing in the pace of the job growth over the past year reflects a decline in the growth of the labor force due to lower immigration and labor force participation, though labor demand has clearly softened as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Other indicators, including job openings, layoffs, hiring, and nominal wage growth, generally show little change in recent months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation has moved up recently and is elevated relative to our 2 percent longer-run goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Estimates based on the consumer price index and other data indicate that total PCE prices rose 3.5 percent over the 12 months ending in March, boosted by the significant rise in global oil prices that has resulted from the conflict in the Middle East.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core PCE prices rose 3.2 percent over the 12 months ending in March.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: This relatively high rate largely reflects the effects of tariffs on prices in the goods sector.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Near-term measures of inflation expectations have risen this year, likely because of the substantial rise in oil prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Most measures of longer-term expectations remain consistent with our 2 percent inflation goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our monetary policy actions are guided by our dual mandate to promote maximum employment and stable prices for the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At today’s meeting, the Committee decided to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 3½ to 3¾ percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The economic outlook remains highly uncertain, and the conflict in the Middle East has added to this uncertainty.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In the near term, higher energy prices will push up overall inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Beyond that, the scope and duration of potential effects on the economy remain unclear, as does the future course of the conflict itself.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We will continue to monitor the risks to both sides of our dual mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We are well positioned to determine the extent and timing of additional adjustments to our policy rate based on the incoming data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Monetary policy is not on a preset course, and we will make our decisions on a meeting-by-meeting basis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: This is my last press conference as Chair, and I will close with a few thoughts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: First, I want to congratulate Kevin Warsh on his advancement out of the Senate Banking Committee this morning.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: This is an important step forward, and I wish him well as that process continues.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The Federal Reserve exists for one fundamental purpose: to foster the economic conditions in which American families and businesses can thrive—stable prices, a strong job market, and a financial system they can depend on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Every decision we make—whether about interest rates, or regulatory and supervisory matters, or other issues—is made in service of that purpose.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our decisions reflect the collective judgment of the Board of Governors and the Federal Open Market Committee—colleagues who demonstrate analytical rigor, principled judgment, and a genuine commitment to the public interest.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our collaborative and deliberative process has long reflected a shared commitment to finding common ground in service to our mission.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: This institution is resilient, capable, and staffed by professionals of extraordinary talent and exceptional dedication.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It has been a privilege to serve alongside so many great public servants at the Board of Governors and around the Federal Reserve System.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The Fed’s work is only as effective as the public’s understanding of it, and you, the press, are essential to keeping the public informed about what we do and why.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The people we serve benefit from your careful reporting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I welcomed the announcement last Friday by the U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia that she had closed the criminal investigation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: She also noted, however, that she would not hesitate to restart the investigation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Over the weekend, the Department of Justice provided assurances that they will not reopen the investigation unless there is a criminal referral from the Fed’s Inspector General.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, absent such a referral, if they do appeal the recent court decision, they would not seek as part of that appeal to restart the investigation or send new subpoenas.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I have said that I will not leave the Board until this investigation is well and truly over, with transparency and finality, and I stand by that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’m encouraged by recent developments, and I’m watching the remaining steps in this process carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: My decisions on these matters will continue to be guided entirely by what I believe is in the best interest of the institution and the people we serve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: After my term as Chair ends on May 15, I will continue to serve as a Governor for a period of time to be determined.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I plan to keep a low profile as a Governor.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There is only ever one Chair of the Federal Reserve Board.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: When Kevin Warsh is confirmed and sworn in, he will be that Chair.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Once sworn in as Board Chair, his new colleagues will elect him to chair the FOMC as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As I regularly point out from this podium, our success in delivering on our goals matters for all Americans.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I am confident that the Fed will continue to do its work with objectivity, integrity, and a deep commitment to serve the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thank you, and I look forward to your questions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Sure.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you know, my concern is really about the series of legal attacks on the Fed which threaten our ability to conduct monetary policy without considering political factors.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I want to note here this has nothing whatever to do with verbal criticism by elected officials.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’ve never suggested that such verbal criticism is a problem, and neither has anyone else here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But these legal actions by the Administration are unprecedented in our 113-year history, and there are ongoing threats of additional such actions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I worry that these attacks are battering the institution and putting at risk the thing that really matters to the public—which is the ability to conduct monetary policy without taking into consideration political factors.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It is so important for our economy, for the people that we serve, that they can depend over time on a central bank that operates that way, free of political influence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s part of the absolute foundation of this amazing economy that we have.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s just one of the many reasons why the U.S. economy is the envy of the world.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That piece of institutional architecture separates successful countries from unsuccessful countries.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It is extremely important—not for the people who work at the Fed at any given time, but for the people that we serve—that the Fed remain able to conduct monetary policy in a way that doesn’t get pulled into politics, trying to help or hurt any particular politician or political party.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s critical for the people that we serve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In terms of when I would leave, I will leave when I think it’s appropriate to do so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t see that at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As I mentioned, you know, I’m literally staying because of the actions that have been taken.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I had long planned to be retiring.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, the things that have happened, really, in the last three months have, I think, left me no choice but to stay until I see them through at least that long.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, in addition, I don’t see how this will interfere.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: My intention is not to interfere.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, I was a Governor for almost six years, and the tradition is, at the Fed, that Governors who understand how difficult the role of Chair is—and as a soon-to-be former Chair, I do understand how hard it is to get consensus with 19 strong-minded people—you work with the Chair, you try to be heard, but also collaborate with the Chair and try to support the Chair when you can.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: When you can’t, you can’t.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I think that’s the attitude that people generally take.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s the attitude that I’ll take.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you know, I would look at it this way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: For a long time, we’ve been working on the hypothesis, really, that tariff, tariffs would lead to a one-time price increase and that that would go away over time—in other words, that there would be no further change, so measured inflation wouldn’t reflect that higher level, going up more and more.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it’s time for that to happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we really do expect that to be happening in the next two quarters.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’ll be watching very carefully to see that what we’ve thought all along would happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s the kind of critical part of the forecast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We need to really see that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: With, with energy, it’s so hard to say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mentioned, you know, in, you know, sort of the textbook [analysis], you would “look through” an oil shock because they tend to be short lived and they tend to revert.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And monetary policy works with long and variable lags, so, you know, you wouldn’t necessarily react right away.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think that is all the more true, given that we’re several years above 2 percent inflation, and that we’re already “looking through” the tariff shock.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think we’re going to be very cautious about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s—but the, you know, the question about looking through energy really is not in front of us right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It hasn’t even peaked yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I think we’d want to see the back side of that and progress on tariffs before we even thought about, about reducing rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that was—as you will recall, we had a discussion about that at the last meeting, and we talked about it in the press conference after the March meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We had the same today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We had quite a vigorous discussion about that very issue and the guidance and “is it still appropriate” and that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I would say that the, you know, number of people on the Committee who either could support that language change changing to a more neutral stance so that the hike is as likely as a cut—that number has increased over the intermeeting period.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it’s easy to see why.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You see inflation has moved up over the interim a bit—core inflation’s 3.2 [percent] now—moving albeit just a little bit in the wrong direction.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we know that there will be, you know, that there’s headline inflation coming out of the Gulf and we don’t know how much that will be, we just—we’re going to need to see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it makes all the sense in the world that people would look at that and we’d have a vigorous discussion about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You saw that three people dissented over the language.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think all of those people agreed with the rate decision.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So the majority of the Committee did not want to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, and I was—I didn’t think we needed to do it at this meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we have so much to learn, there’s so much uncertainty about the path ahead, there doesn’t need to be any rush to make that decision now because, you know, what happens in the next 30, 60 days, even by the next meeting, could really change the picture around that—around that language.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you know, it was a—it’s a close—it’s a much closer thing on the Committee than it was in March.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, that makes all the sense in the world, it seems to me.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I wouldn’t want to guess.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know—well, first of all, we’re going to have new leadership, in all likelihood, by then.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And new leadership is going to have a very important role to play in that, so I won’t be standing here at this podium to answer your questions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As I mentioned, that’s all I can really say is that we had a great discussion about that today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s a—you know, it’s got—it’s gotten to be a better question in the interim period.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We had the discussion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: A majority are still on the page of not feeling the need to move to that level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I—that’s where I am.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I get it, though.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, at a certain point, you would move.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that, that conceivably could come as soon as the next meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I’m not going to give him any advice through you today here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I’ve—you know, I think communications generally is—I think every incoming Chair takes a look at communications, and it’s a very healthy thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, communications is—it’s very complex, and, you know, you can always be looking at new things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And if that happens—it feels like it’s going to happen—that’s a completely appropriate thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I haven’t seen him since seeing him at a dinner in January, where I congratulated him and had a nice chat with him.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Haven’t seen him.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t know what a normal process is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, the last process was with Janet Yellen, with whom I had worked for six years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so it was—you know, we were sitting down the hall from each other, so it was a very different thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think this is and will be a very normal, standard kind of a—kind of a transition process.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s what I expect.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I have every reason to think it will be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I wasn’t thinking of it as such.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, no, not really.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, I’m thinking more of the other things I mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t know the answer to that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, what we—so what we experienced in, in the teens—the mid-teens was really low levels of unemployment for a long period of time and no reaction from inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Now, we all took—very much took notice of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We also noticed that the biggest wage gains were going to people at the bottom end of the income spectrum.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we had many, many reports of—I mean, it felt like a fairly stable equilibrium.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And a lot of benefits were flowing to people at the bottom end of the income spectrum, including companies were, you know, setting up in, in, you know—people who were confined and, like, training them before they got out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it was a—it was a very healthy sort of set of societal dynamics.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, of course, I think anybody would love to get back to that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t think that anything that happened to create the global pandemic inflation was in any way related to overweighting the employment market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, it was a global shock that happened essentially very, very similarly all over the world [and] that had to do with closing and reopening, stimulus, and all that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, I mean, you could look at a graph of 10 big economies on the page and not know which was the U.S. and which was Germany, France, and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I don’t think that that insight was in any way responsible for the high inflation that we experienced.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, I mean, I think it’s always been a balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You’ve got to—you’ve got to be strong on both of our dual mandates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we just—for example, now we don’t feel that the labor market is at all a source of inflation, so we don’t need to be worrying about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s been a long time since we have had to worry about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, actually, during the pandemic recovery, the labor market was super overheated and tight, and that’s when we had to worry about it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But not now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So people are not saying we need to hike now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: People argue that this is consistent with markets are doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, again, it’s a very fair question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, you know, these changes, there is—you know, it’s a form of forward guidance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And you want to make—you don’t want to make them—you want to make them in a way that will be sustained and continue to make sense and not something you need to take back, you know, fairly quickly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think we just—a group of us, including me, didn’t feel like we needed to be in a hurry on that, that markets are not confused about our reaction function.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t have a problem to solve on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But the other side of the argument is a good argument, too, as I mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s a perfectly good argument to be having, good discussion to be having, so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it came out the way it came out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Not driving my thinking now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, monetary policy is going to get made by, you know, 19 people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There’s a lot of stability there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, if you think about it, any—every new Fed Chair has the same situation, which is you’ve got 18 colleagues on the FOMC, 11 of them vote during any year, and you have to—your job is to create consensus.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s to talk to them, understand them, you know, be inside their thinking, and be able to pull them together and get consensus and move.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s what every Fed Chair has to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I think Kevin Warsh is actually quite well—he has the capabilities, skills to be very good at that, I would think.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think—I’m not so worried about that process.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, I think that’ll work itself out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yeah.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, that’s just something I would never do—you know, the “shadow Chair” thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: No.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, I—it’s—I don’t know what the exact specifics of it will be, but I’m going back to being a Governor.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I respect the role of Chair.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, I was a Chair—I was a Governor for six years, and I know what that’s like.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I know what—and I had a, you know, pretty front row seat, particularly with Chair Yellen, to whom I was close.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I, I worked with Chairman Bernanke for two years, but, you know, I was brand new at that time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I got a sense of what it was.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I had real sympathy for how hard it is to get that group to consensus.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I always felt like I—you know, I don’t want to add to that unnecessarily.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that means try to support the Chairs where the Chair—the direction the Chair wants to go, if you can.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If you can’t, you can’t.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But—and I think that’s the way it’s always worked there because the Chair only has one vote plus the ability to develop consensus.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so that’s why the Chair has the authority, the Chair has, really, is to develop relationships with people and work with them, and then—and then put something forward that has consensus.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I, you know, I propose to be a very constructive participant in that process, really out of respect for the office of the Chair.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, those prospects are real.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Remember, though, our—they’re real.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And the real thing is we’re going to have to wait and see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re going to need to see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And the good news is we think our policy stance is just—is in a very good place for us to wait and see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We, you know, we’re right kind of at the high end of neutral or perhaps mildly restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The labor market shows more and more signs of stability, whereas inflation is kind of misbehaving.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so maybe a little bit of restriction or the high end of neutral is just the right place to be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we can wait here and see—and see how things work out before we act.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’ll see how much that—you know, how much does come through into core.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You see it already in airfares, of course.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But you may see it in many other places.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we just don’t know yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You can develop any number of scenarios that you want, but we really won’t know till we know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, fortunately, we’re in a good place to wait and let things develop.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we, we always said—when we were doing quarterly press conferences, we always said “we can move at any meeting”—but we only ever moved at the quarterly SEP meetings where we had the press conference.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So if you think about it, you know, we—during the pandemic, we were moving, like, a lot at every meeting and sometimes between meetings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And doing that without a press conference, I think, would have been quite challenging.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s become the industry norm.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s the standard.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t know whether that has to remain that way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, I—it’s just something people have become used to.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I do think it’s quite helpful to, you know, to—I mean, I try to deliver a message on behalf of the Committee rather than 18 people—18 other people going out and delivering their message.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it’s, you know, it’s going to be all over the place because we do, thankfully, have widely disparate views.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I’m not going to go into the real small specifics.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But what we found very quickly was that making, making changes—making really large changes, for example, to the dot plot or the SEP, it didn’t have—we couldn’t come up with anything that had really broad support on the Committee.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so we just moved on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We didn’t—we didn’t really do as much on that as we might have.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, I was never the world’s biggest fan of the dot plot, but you can’t—you can’t beat something with nothing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, there’s a—that we’ve looked at a bunch of things and, you know, it’s something, like I said, I think every new Chair is going to look at our suite of communications and think about what would be changes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We are the only major central bank that doesn’t publish a forecast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s because we have a 19-person Committee, and, you know, you try to do it—you try to do that at the Board, that’s hard—at the Committee, that’s hard.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s hard if you do it at the staff.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s, you know, it’s been—it works.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think our communications are fine, but looking at doing it in a different and better way is the most natural thing in the world.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, where we’re at is we think our—really, we think our policy rate is in a good place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If we need to hike, we will certainly signal that, and we will—and we will certainly do it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And if we need to cut, then—or if it’s appropriate to cut, then we’ll signal the opposite.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think we—because we feel like we’re in a good place to move in either direction, nobody’s calling for a hike right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it really is going to depend on how things—how things evolve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, that’s really where it is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, as I mentioned, you know, much closer question this cycle on changing the guidance, but, ultimately, we didn’t.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, you just have to find that out empirically.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, with—given our—the fact that we’re, you know, a big exporter of energy and that our economy is far less energy intensive, oil intensive, than it was during the ’70s, you know, the effects on the United States are really substantially less than those of Western Europe or Asia.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re feeling much greater effects from these things—the effects we’re feeling in, you know, in the current situation currently and in sort of what’s priced in, which is, you know, a relatively quick outcome.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If this goes on for much longer and prices go much higher, then we’ll feel that much more.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, of course, I’m talking about aggregate inflation numbers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We know—we’re very well aware that people are experiencing higher gas prices all over the country now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that hurts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s—and these are—those hikes may continue to happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And other things are going to start to reflect—airline fares I’ve mentioned and other products and services that are dependent upon petroleum and derivatives of petroleum.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: People are going to start to feel that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, the neutral rate is a—we cannot know it with, with certainty.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think pretty close to the neutral rate, yeah.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I always had it, you know, between 3 and 4 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re a little north of 3½ [percent], so that’s well in the range of what I would consider reasonable, but at the higher end of the range of what I would consider reasonable neutral rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, I think you’re—the labor market is still probably cooling off just a little bit.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I don’t think there’s much of a case for—any case, really—for, for policy looking, you know, meaningfully restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Maybe mildly restrictive or neutral, I would say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, the thing to remember is we have always had vigorous debates, and they’re excellent debates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I have to say, they’re—they’ve been really good.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’re in an unusually difficult situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’ve really had four supply shocks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You can— actually, you can say more than four, but, at a minimum, we’ve—we had the pandemic, we had the invasion of Ukraine, we had tariffs, and now we have Iran and the oil, you know, the oil spike.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So those—every, every supply shock has the capability of, right, driving inflation up and unemployment up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, you’re—it’s—the central bank has a really hard time knowing what to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So the right thing to do is to try to balance the achievement of those two goals, and that’s what our framework calls for us to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But these are really tough, difficult judgments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You’ve got to have a forecast for each variable.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You’ve got to think how long it’s going to take to get back to target.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You’ve got to think how restrictive or not is policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s only natural that you have a range of views on the Committee.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, people are going to see it different ways, they’re going to have different risk tolerances and that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, if everybody agreed, that would be—that would be surprising.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I think it’s only—it’s partly a function of the extraordinarily challenging set of supply shocks that we’ve been dealing with now for five, six years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So he testified very strongly to that effect in his hearing, and I’ll take him at his word.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t know what gas prices are going to do for the rest of the year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it will depend on how long the Strait remains closed and how quickly it can be reopened and that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, remember, when gas prices go up, that’s disposable income coming out of people’s pockets, so they’re going to spend less on other things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So there will be a hit to GDP.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s a, you know, it’s a question whether spending, you know, goes down to offset the inflationary effects.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s not—the answer isn’t obvious ex ante whether you—whether you should move your rate over because of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ll have to see how it evolves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’ll stand on what I said earlier.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, it’s, you know, it’s—to a significant extent, it is the law.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, we’ve had to go to court to—successfully, so far—to defend it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, you know, the law does create a setting in which the Fed can and is directed to make monetary policy without consideration of political factors.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so part of it is the law.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But it goes beyond that, though.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There’s a set of customs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There’s a boundary line between the Fed and the Administration, between the Fed and the Treasury Department.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we need to respect those—continue to respect those boundaries about what the Fed is responsible for and what the Treasury is responsible for and what the rest of the Administration’s responsible.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So some of it is legal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In fact, it’s all legal at the end of the day.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But there—it’s more than just monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We, you know, we don’t—we don’t want to use our tools to—we haven’t wanted to use our tools to achieve goals that are really clearly outside our mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Every Administration looks at our tools and thinks that would be good to repurpose those to serve other purposes, but that gets dragged—that’s dragging us into politics and into fiscal policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’ve resisted that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Look, I think it’s at risk.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, I think these, these you know, these legal assaults, if you will—as I mentioned, you know, the institution is being battered over these things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re having to resort to, you know, the courts to, to enforce our legal, you know, it’s not so much independence, it’s really the ability to do monetary—to make monetary policy without political considerations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s what we’re talking about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’ve had to do that, and we’ve been successful so far, but that’s not over.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: None of that is concluded yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it’s, you know, it’s really important.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s not about—it’s not about people who work at the Fed or the institution—it’s about the benefits of a central bank that makes decisions based on analysis and our best thinking rather than, you know, trying to help or hurt politicians.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s, you know—there’s a bright line between central banks who do one and do the other.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And successful countries have uniformly—successful, advanced-economy countries have a really strong set of protections around their central bank just for that reason.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s what it’s all about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, I think—I am confident, as I said in my remarks, that the Fed will continue to make its decision based on analysis—rigorous analysis—and not on political considerations, but we’ve had to fight for it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I, you know, I’d like to think that—you know, I’d like to think we can get out of that era and go back to respecting, you know, what the law says and what custom has been, which is to, you know, let the Fed do our thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re, you know, we’re not—we’re— it’s a—it’s an institution full of human beings who work super hard to get things right for the benefit of the public.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re all human.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Don’t expect perfection.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But do expect us to make, you know, decisions without political considerations and the very best analysis we can bring.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think that—I don’t want to report on what my colleagues think.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They can—they can speak for themselves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, you know, yeah, there are—there are widespread concerns that these things may continue.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s all—that’s all I’ll say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, and that would be a problem.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we try to be good stewards of the public’s money, and efficient.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And Chris, in particular—Chris Waller is particularly passionate about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Of course, so are the Reserve—so are the presidents.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, it’s a question of how do you accomplish it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We, of course—and Chris said this in his speech—we, you know, we want 12 strong independent central banks with their own staffs and their own monetary policy views and all that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, you know, there are things that are done in all 12 which could well be done at 1 much more efficiently and with cost savings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so there’s a back-and-forth going on on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But everybody, everybody’s on the same page.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The other thing he touched on was the idea of removing Reserve Bank presidents from office over different, different views on monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I would—I would just agree with him so strongly that that would be the beginning of the end of, of the Fed’s ability to, to make monetary policy independently.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If every Administration could come in and do that, you’re just another cabinet agency at that point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s not something that I would support.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Chris said the same thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, I’m going to just say that that’s for—that’s for someone else to say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’ll give you a mulligan on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we’re committed to bring inflation back down to 2 percent and sustainably.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s our goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we will—we’ll stick at it until that happens.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We keep getting—these events keep happening which keep driving up costs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, the best thing we can do is to use our tools to guide inflation back down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think trying to get there really quickly could be very costly in terms of job loss and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we try to get there over time in a way that does the least damage possible.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, our commitment to that is never-ending and unshakable.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t know that you can be “awfully” resilient—so it’s actually quite resilient, I would say, because it’s a positive thing, if I can—if I can have that amendment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yeah, you know, growth is really solid across our economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Some of that is that consumer spending is hanging in pretty well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The most recent data are good.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And some of it is just the apparently insatiable demand for data centers all over the United States.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So a lot of business investment going into building data centers, and every reason to think that that continues.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So you’ve got an economy that’s growing at 2 percent or better.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: PDFP, which is private domestic final purchases, which is really a better signal of, of momentum in the economy, is actually higher than that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s, you know, that’s a positive thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If you look at the unemployment rate, it’s 4.3 [percent], so that’s a low rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s pretty close to mainstream estimates of the natural rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve been there for a long time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s—it doesn’t feel like a good labor market to some who don’t have jobs because quits are really low, hires are really low, and there’s effectively no new net job creation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s, that’s—you know, in a sense, the labor market is in balance, but it’s an unusual and uncomfortable kind of a balance where people who don’t have jobs will have a hard time breaking in unless somebody quits their job.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s pretty good.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, inflation is the thing we need to work on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it’s partly tariffs, which we think—we think that that inflation should subside over the course of this year because it’s kind of a one-time increase, it shouldn’t be repeated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that should start happening pretty soon.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The energy inflation that we’re getting should go through fairly quickly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’ll just have to see how that works out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In the meantime, you know, we think our policy stance is in a good place for us to hold and wait developments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think that, you know, the center is moving toward a more neutral place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s sort of what markets are saying, too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I just think, you know, there’s a lot of signaling going on when you change guidance like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so we just—I guess a majority of us didn’t feel like we needed to send a signal on that right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And—but maybe it’ll come to that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And the reason is because, you know, we’re kind of waiting to see what happens with, with events in the Middle East and what are the implications of those events for the U.S. economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So there was just a—there’s a group who feels like we don’t need to be in a hurry to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We get it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, of course, we will move to a hiking bias if we want to hike, and we’ll move to a neutral bias before that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But there was a difference over whether to do it at this meeting—at a meeting at which all but one of us agreed that the—that the rate decision was correct, which was not to move.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I want to stay until I—I will stay until it’s—I feel it’s appropriate for me to leave.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, yes, that is—that is really what is driving this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’m not—I’m not looking to be, you know, a high-profile dissident or anything like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’m more looking at the other aspects of this and wanting to see that things have calmed down and are returning to a traditional model of working with the people that you have and bringing them to consensus and respecting that consensus.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s what—that’s what I’m hoping to see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yeah, it’s hard.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I wouldn’t want to single out individual things at this point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, I’ll just say, you know, we—all of us together have consistently tried to do what we think is best for the American people based on our tools and our objectives that Congress has given us.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s been very challenging because we’ve been in a situation of supply shock—supply shocks, really, for six years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s just a very different situation than—for a very long time, what the Fed and other central banks were doing all the time was demand management.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, and there was always the inflation mandate, but inflation was low for 25 years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So this is a very different world and a much more challenging one where you have to balance the two objectives.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, by the way, central banks that have an inflation mandate have to do exactly the same thing because they’re balancing economic activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s been challenging.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’ve, you know, we’ve tried to do our very best through these really challenging times.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I’m really proud of the work that I’ve done, that my—that my colleagues and I have done during these, these years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So every major advanced economy in the world has made the same decision the United States has made.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that is that they want to take the making of monetary policy, the setting of interest rates to support the economy, to achieve maximum employment and price stability—they want to take that out of the direct control of elected politicians.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And the reason is elected politicians are always running for election and they’ll always want low rates, and that will lead to inflation over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So after, you know, literally centuries of experience with that, the whole world moved to the different model.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it’s worked great.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, this is—this is the era in which inflation was under control for 40 years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Then we had the pandemic—inflation everywhere in the world.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And now we have inflation that had gone pretty much all the way back to target—really close to all the way back to target and now is being buffeted by the energy shock in the U.S., buffeted by the—by the tariff shock as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But what I would say to the general public is—that’s the backstory—is that don’t think about an institution being independent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Think about it this way—that you want people to make monetary policy and set interest rates to benefit the general public and to try to achieve economic goals, which are maximum employment and price stability, and focus only on that and ignore political considerations, completely ignore them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s—this isn’t bipartisan, this is nonpartisan.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we want to just—we just work directly for the American people doing these things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t think, “Oh, this—I want to do this because the President says it’s a good idea or because there’s an election coming up and I want to—I want to speed up or slow down the economy.” I mean, that—think about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If that’s—if that—if that’s what we were doing, we’d have no credibility, markets would lose faith in us and our ability to control inflation and have any respect would be, you know, would be gone.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And let me say—whatever people say, the markets believe that we will produce 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If you look at longer-run expectations, markets believe that—there’s no sense in which our credibility in the markets has weakened.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s just not the case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s—people do get it that this is our commitment and that we will achieve it and it’s priced in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If you disagree with that, then you can go ahead and bet against the markets.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But the markets are pricing in Fed credibility.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You don’t see—you don’t see it in spending yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You really don’t.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, as one of your colleagues said, the economy has been resilient—it really has—not just this time, but it’s been remarkably resilient for some years now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The U.S. economy has just powered through shock after shock.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And consumers are still spending.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s what—that’s what the banks will tell you, credit card companies will tell you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The retail sales numbers that we got most recently—people are still spending.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, how long can that go on in a world where—if gas prices were to go up a bunch more, that’s taking otherwise spendable money out of people’s pockets.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, right now, we don’t actually see much slowdown in—yet from—certainly, none from this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But you think logically you will because people have a certain amount of money they spend.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If they’re spending 25 percent more on gas or something like that, then, you know, that’s going to come out of other spending.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we—again, we don’t see it yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So all of those things are in—are in the models that we use to calculate inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we—you know, they’re just parts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You can ask about anything like that, and they are—they have a place—the staff has a place where they’re looking at that and pricing in what will happen with higher prices and that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The effects are not that big yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we’re a huge economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The import sector is only 10 percent of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’re not like a European country where 50 percent of the external—of GDP is in the external sector.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re also, you know, as I mentioned, we’re an oil exporter, so we’re not feeling the same kind of pain—and we’re not likely to feel the same kind of pain—that economies in Western Europe and, certainly, in Asia are feeling.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Anyway, thank you very much, everyone.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I won’t see you next time.
